### Libraries
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(car)
library(lme4)
library(nlme)
library(DHARMa)
library(rgl)
# library(remef)
library(dplyr)
```


### Load data and create factors

```{r}
behavior = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/behavior_analysis/behavior_data_matrix_all.csv")
# behavior = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/behavior_analysis/behavior_data_matrix_1sthalfpred.csv")
# behavior = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/behavior_analysis/behavior_data_matrix_2ndhalfpred.csv")
behavior$resp = behavior$resp - 1
# behavior = behavior[behavior$X2.5Hz==0,]
behavior = behavior[behavior$block>=3,]

behavior$trial_nb <- as.integer(substr(behavior$stim_name, 6, 8))

behavior$note_rate = (behavior %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c("X2.5Hz", "X3.5Hz", "X4.5Hz", "X5.5Hz", "X6.5Hz"),
               names_to = "note_rate") %>%
  filter(value == 1) %>%
  select(note_rate))$note_rate

# u-shape parameter for note rate
behavior$u_param = 0
# behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X2.5Hz',]$u_param = 2.25
# behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X3.5Hz',]$u_param = 0.25
# behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X4.5Hz',]$u_param = 0.25
# behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X5.5Hz',]$u_param = 2.25
# behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X6.5Hz',]$u_param = 6.25
behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X2.5Hz',]$u_param = 1.5
behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X3.5Hz',]$u_param = 0.5
behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X4.5Hz',]$u_param = 0.5
behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X5.5Hz',]$u_param = 1.5
behavior[behavior$note_rate=='X6.5Hz',]$u_param = 2.5

behavior$rep = (behavior %>%
                        pivot_longer(cols = c("rep1", "rep2", "rep3"),
                                     names_to = "rep") %>%
                        filter(value == 1) %>%
                        select(rep))$rep

# add efficiency as correct*rs (with incorrect as -1 and correct as 1)
# behavior$efficiency = 0
# behavior[behavior$correct==0,]$efficiency = -1
# behavior[behavior$correct==1,]$efficiency = 1
# behavior$efficiency = behavior$rs * behavior$efficiency

behavior$subject = as.factor(behavior$subject)
behavior$stim_identity = as.factor(behavior$stim_identity)
behavior$note_rate = as.factor(behavior$note_rate)
behavior$rep = as.factor(behavior$rep)
behavior$onset_type = as.factor(behavior$onset_type)

behavior$beta_7s = behavior$beta_7s - min(behavior$beta_7s) + 0.001

# behavior = behavior[behavior$surprise_mean_paulrnn < 0.19,]
# behavior = behavior[behavior$surprise_mean_paulrnn < 0.14,]

behavior$meg = 1  # subject group

# keep only stim that have 3 presentations (in block 8 and 9)
behavior <- behavior %>%
  group_by(subject, stim_identity) %>%  
  mutate(n_per_subject = n()) %>%  # Count occurrences per subject
  ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(stim_identity) %>%  
  mutate(keep_stim = any(n_per_subject >= 3)) %>%  # Check if at least one subject has ≥3 presentations
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(keep_stim | block < 8)
```

```{r}
hist(behavior$surprise_mean_paulrnn, breaks=30)
hist(behavior$max_surprise, breaks=30)
hist(behavior$std_surprise, breaks=30)
```


### Centering
```{r}
scale_columns = function(data, columns) {

  for (col in columns) {
    if (col %in% names(data)) {
      scaled_col <- as.vector(scale(data[[col]], scale=TRUE))
      data[[col]] <- scaled_col
    } else {
      warning(paste("Column", col, "not found in the dataframe. Skipping..."))
    }
  }

  return(data)
}

columns_to_scale = names(behavior)[sapply(behavior, is.numeric)]  # keep numeric columns
columns_to_scale = columns_to_scale[!columns_to_scale %in% c("X", "onset_type", "rep1", "rep2", "rep3", "X2.5Hz", "X3.5Hz", "X4.5Hz", "X5.5Hz", "X6.5Hz", "resp", "correct", "beta_7s", "hrv", "rs", "meg")]
behavior = scale_columns(behavior, columns_to_scale)

# behavior$surprise_distance = (behavior$surprise_mean_paulrnn)**2
behavior$surprise_distance = abs(behavior$surprise_mean_paulrnn)
```

```{r}
behavior_rep12 = behavior[(behavior$rep1==1) | (behavior$rep2==1),]
```

## Modelling
### Linear models tests
```{r}
model = lm(correct~surprise_mean_paulrnn, data=behavior)
summary(model)
AIC(model)
model = lm(beta_7s~surprise_mean_paulrnn, data=behavior_rep2[behavior$correct==1,])
summary(model)
AIC(model)
model = lm(heart_pulses~surprise_mean_paulrnn, data=behavior_rep2[behavior$correct==1,])
summary(model)
AIC(model)
model = lm(rs~surprise_mean_paulrnn, data=behavior_rep2[behavior$correct==1,])
summary(model)
AIC(model)
```

### Assumptions checking
1) All of the observations are independent - this must be addressed at the design and collection stages
2) The response variable (and thus the residuals) should be normally distributed
3) The response variable should be equally varied (variance should not be related to mean as these are supposed to be estimated separately)
4) The relationship between the linear predictor (right hand side of the regression formula) and the link function should be linear. A scatterplot with smoother can be useful for identifying possible non-linearity.

### Multicolinearity check
```{r}
vif(lm(correct~surprise_mean_paulrnn*entropy_pitch_paulrnn*entropy_timing_paulrnn-surprise_mean_paulrnn:entropy_pitch_paulrnn:entropy_timing_paulrnn+
       pitch+pitch_interval+onset_type+block+position_in_block+rs+gmsi+note_rate,
       data=behavior_rep2))
```

```{r}
model = lm(correct~surprise_mean_paulrnn*entropy_pitch_paulrnn*entropy_timing_paulrnn-surprise_mean_paulrnn:entropy_pitch_paulrnn:entropy_timing_paulrnn+
       pitch+pitch_interval+onset_type+block+position_in_block+rs+gmsi+note_rate, 
       data=behavior_rep2)
summary(model)
AIC(model)
plot(model)
avPlot(model, "surprise_mean_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
avPlot(model, "entropy_pitch_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
avPlot(model, "entropy_timing_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
avPlot(model, "entropy_pitch_paulrnn:entropy_timing_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
avPlot3d(model, "entropy_pitch_paulrnn", "entropy_timing_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
rglwidget()
```

### GLM
```{r}
model = glm(correct~surprise_mean_paulrnn*entropy_pitch_paulrnn*entropy_timing_paulrnn-surprise_mean_paulrnn:entropy_pitch_paulrnn:entropy_timing_paulrnn+
       pitch+pitch_interval+onset_type+block+position_in_block+rs+gmsi+note_rate,
       data=behavior_rep2, family="binomial")
summary(model)
plot(model)
avPlot(model, "entropy_pitch_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
avPlot(model, "entropy_timing_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
avPlot(model, "entropy_pitch_paulrnn:entropy_timing_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
avPlot3d(model, "entropy_pitch_paulrnn", "entropy_timing_paulrnn", id=FALSE)
rglwidget()
```

### individual pred features and group testing
Good results are only obtained when 2.5Hz trials are removed. This should be justified (in different analyses, we saw that 2.5Hz was behaving weirdly). Effects seem consistent but harder to interpret when adding 2.5Hz.

The note_rate is better as a fixed effect rather than random effect and adding random slopes for subjects doesn't improve the model (this was tested on rep 2 only).

This is confirmed by running one model for rep1 and one model for rep23. In rep 1, only timing is significant. In rep 2-3, all predictive features are significant (timing ns. but close). This suggests the following:
- Pieces that are uncertain in terms of content (entropy pitch) are harder to encode, as the statistical process generating them is harder to reduce to a convenient neural dimension.
- Timing predictability is harder to interpret, as it is significant in both new and old trials with opposite effects. As it is associated to high rhythmic regularity, it is easier to process in rep 1. Why does it have a negative effect in old trials? In line with Sherman 2022, it could be that pieces that lead to strong expectations are more likely to be forgotten, because we prioritize the storage of experiences that lead to weak expectations.
- Accordingly, surprising pieces are easier to encode into memory, as surprise appear in bad predictions (the relationship with the strength of prediction should be studied because surprise also happens when predictions are strong but violated).

The interaction surprise*timing is negative in rep23, suggesting that the effect surprise has on memory is reduced in predictable pieces.

Effects in rep 2 and rep 3 are similar, but increase with rep. Adding the interaction between surprise and timing shows that the individual effect of timing predictability decreases with rep whereas the effect of surprise increases.
=> In rep 1 (and still a bit in rep 2), pieces are not encoded yet. Thus, since predictable pieces (high timing) are easier to process, they are consistently categorized as new (not encoded yet), whereas unpredictable pieces are randomly categorized. Once encoded, the timing effect disappears because performance depends on the memory encoding, thus surprise (which facilitates encoding) becomes dominant.

Hypothesis: the decision is made early in the pieces, so the average predictive features of the first half should have more effect on performance.
- First half vs whole mean: effect of surprise and timing increase (in terms of p-value), but entropy pitch is not significant anymore
- First half vs second half:

Encoding vs recalling distinction, how to disentangle?

Design an online exp to answer the quesitons?

Model of resp (not correct):

(See next cell) There is a very significant and consistent bias to respond "old" at faster note rates. True across reps.
Onset type 2 (smooth) is biased towards "old".
=> If rate and smoothness are seen as an other form of complexity that is hard to encode, subjects may resolve to their bias for the experiment, which is 2/3 "old". If this is true, both biases should increase with the experiment time, as subjects learn this experimental bias (unconsciously?).
WRONG: the bias was coming from block 2 (unbalanced)....... The actual bias is negative (around 1/2 of 'old' response) and does not evolve with blocks, suggesting that participants simply resolve to "new" when they do not recognize a piece.
But there is still a consistent bias for "old" with higher rates and smooth onsets (which effects do not significantly change across the experiment). They are consistent across reps, except onset type which is ns. in rep1 (but in the same direction, may be a false negative, especially because it appears in model of correct) , suggesting that smooth pieces are easier to encode? No, it is more likely that it is confounded with already encoded pieces, because smooth pieces are closer. It may be the same with fast rate, as they have more notes, they have a higher memory load? Confusion between a new and an already encoded piece has to appear in fast rates and smooth onsets, otherwise the effect would not be present in rep 1.

Do a distance analysis showing that smooth pieces are closer to one another that sharp pieces. For rate, distance is not ideal because it may be the encoding quality that is bad.
If it is a confusion effect, should it increase with block (in rep1 only)?
Distinguish between two possibilities: different encoding capacity between conditions, or different confusions between conditions?

The behavior for onset shows that d' and percent correct are inverse: sharp has better d', and better percent in rep 1, but smooth has better percent in rep 2 and 3. Again, this suggest a confusion effect in smooth. Reaction speed is a bit higher in smooth (in all rep), again suggesting a higher confidence and thus a real feeling of recognizing the pieces (confusion).
But it could be the opposite: smooth is easier to encode and remember (high percent in rep2-3), and sharp is very hard to encode so most of the time it is not remembered (high percent in rep1)

Plot of biases over blocks: the average bias stays close to chance level 50% (even if the design is 2/3), suggesting that participants are conservative and say 'new' when they are uncertain (otherwise the bias would be higher than 0.5). The ramping over blocks of false positive in rep1 suggests a confusion effect: pieces are counfounded with already encoded ones as the number of encoded information in working memory increases. The different speeds of ramping in rep1 trials show that some conditions are easier to process/separate/precisely encode than others. 
- For the onset shape, smooth pieces are more confounded that sharp ones. 
- For note rates, the higher ramping effects are for 2.5 and 6.5Hz, discarding the hypothesis that it is purely due to memory load of notes (higher rates have more notes). In fact, the ramps seem to follow a U-shape, with 4.5Hz showing the lowest increase in false positive over the blocks, which is exactly in line with Assaneo and Poeppel 2018.
Importantly, rep 2 and rep 3 do not seem to show a significant decrease in hit rate across the experiment, suggesting that the change in bias is driven by rep1 trials, thus purely driven by false positive, in line with an increase of confusion.

Rep1 greatly predicts rep2, which greatly predicts rep3.

Model of correct:

Effects of rate and onset type explained in resp (visible and significant in correct). All effects are similar when adding the 2.5Hz condition, but the effect of rate is non-linear, maybe with a U-shape centered on 3.5Hz/4.5Hz.
No interaction surprise-timing. Interaction surprise-entropy_pitch
- rep 1: positive effect surprise and timing predictability, negative effect of entropy_pitch
- rep 2: negative effect of timing predictability, reduced compared to rep 1.
- rep 3: positive effect of surprise, negative effect of pitch entropy, close to signif negative effect of interaction surprise-entropy_pitch
=> predictable pieces are easier to detect as new whereas unpredictable ones are confounded with already encoded ones. The effect should increase with block in rep 1 (no)
=> surprising pieces are easier to encode and easier to detect as new.
=> pieces with high content (pitch) uncertainty are harder to encode. Should increase with block in rep1? (no)
=> surprise and pitch uncertainty synergize beyond their individual effects: surprise in predictable context is even more salient and weighted down in uncertain context, in line with the predictive coding theory: precision weighting of the prediction error.

Removing block from the dependent variables removes surprise and entropy pitch in rep 1, and adds the interaction effect in rep 3.

Test the last point by transforming the features to a non-ambiguous measure of predictability: negative half-wave corrected versions of the normalized surprise and entropy, multiplication, and normalization again. The opposite (positive half-wave) should be also done and show that it doesn't improve the model as well. Again the effect should increase with block in rep 1

Averaging predictive features over different trial windows:
- [0, 4]: effects conserved in all reps. In rep 1, surprise is almost signif with a negative effect, could it explain next line?
- [4, 8]: effects disappear in rep 1, in rep 2 only NEGATIVE effect of surprise, effects conserved in rep 3

# sEEG analysis

### Load data and create factors

```{r}
behavior_seeg = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/behavior_analysis/seeg_behavior/behavior_seeg_data_matrix.csv")
# behavior_seeg = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/behavior_analysis/seeg_behavior/behavior_seeg_data_matrix_all_trials.csv")
behavior_seeg = behavior_seeg[!(is.na(behavior_seeg$resp) | behavior_seeg$resp==""), ]  # remove empty response, due to multiple button presses with different values
behavior_seeg$resp = behavior_seeg$resp - 1
# behavior_seeg = behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$trial>15,]

behavior_seeg$note_rate = (behavior_seeg %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c("X2.5Hz", "X3.5Hz", "X4.5Hz", "X5.5Hz", "X6.5Hz", "X7.5Hz"),
               names_to = "note_rate") %>%
  filter(value == 1) %>%
  select(note_rate))$note_rate

# u-shape parameter for note rate
behavior_seeg$u_param = 0
behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$note_rate=='X2.5Hz',]$u_param = 1.5
behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$note_rate=='X3.5Hz',]$u_param = 0.5
behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$note_rate=='X4.5Hz',]$u_param = 0.5
behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$note_rate=='X5.5Hz',]$u_param = 1.5
behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$note_rate=='X6.5Hz',]$u_param = 2.5
behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$note_rate=='X7.5Hz',]$u_param = 3.5

behavior_seeg$rep = (behavior_seeg %>%
                        pivot_longer(cols = c("rep1", "rep2"),
                                     names_to = "rep") %>%
                        filter(value == 1) %>%
                        select(rep))$rep

behavior_seeg$subject = as.factor(behavior_seeg$subject)
behavior_seeg$stim_identity = as.factor(behavior_seeg$stim_identity)
behavior_seeg$note_rate = as.factor(behavior_seeg$note_rate)
behavior_seeg$rep = as.factor(behavior_seeg$rep)
behavior_seeg$onset_type = as.factor(behavior_seeg$onset_type)
behavior_seeg$seeg_block = as.factor(behavior_seeg$seeg_block)

behavior_seeg$precision_weighted_pe = behavior_seeg$surprise_possum_paulrnn / behavior_seeg$entropy_pitch_paulrnn
behavior_seeg$precision_weighted_pe_timing = behavior_seeg$surprise_possum_paulrnn / behavior_seeg$entropy_timing_paulrnn
```

### Centering
```{r}
scale_columns = function(data, columns) {

  for (col in columns) {
    if (col %in% names(data)) {
      scaled_col <- as.vector(scale(data[[col]], scale=TRUE))
      data[[col]] <- scaled_col
    } else {
      warning(paste("Column", col, "not found in the dataframe. Skipping..."))
    }
  }

  return(data)
}

columns_to_scale = names(behavior_seeg)[sapply(behavior_seeg, is.numeric)]  # keep numeric columns
columns_to_scale = columns_to_scale[!columns_to_scale %in% c("X", "onset_type", "seeg_block", "rep1", "rep2", "X2.5Hz", "X3.5Hz", "X4.5Hz", "X5.5Hz", "X6.5Hz", "X7.5Hz", "resp", "correct", "meg", "trial_since_rep1")]
behavior_seeg = scale_columns(behavior_seeg, columns_to_scale)

# behavior_seeg$surprise_distance = (behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn)**2
behavior_seeg$surprise_distance = abs(behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn)

# behavior_seeg = behavior_seeg[behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn <= 2,]

behavior_seeg$low_surprise = ifelse(behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn < 0, behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn, 0)
behavior_seeg$high_surprise = ifelse(behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn > 0, behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn, 0)
```

### barplot correct~surprise
```{r}
boxplot(correct~subject, data=behavior_seeg)

quantiles = quantile(behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn, probs=seq(0, 1, 0.1))

behavior_seeg$bin_surprise = cut(behavior_seeg$surprise_mean_paulrnn, breaks = 3, labels=FALSE)
ggplot(behavior_seeg, aes(x = factor(bin_surprise), y = correct)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar", fill = "skyblue") +

  labs(x = "Binned surprise", y = "Proportion correct") +
```

### Simple logistic regression and diagnostic plots
```{r}
model = glm(correct ~ note_rate + rep + surprise_mean_paulrnn + I(surprise_mean_paulrnn**2), data = behavior_seeg, family = binomial(link='logit'))
summary(model)

ggplot(behavior_seeg, aes(x = fitted(model), y = residuals(model, type = "deviance"))) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Deviance Residuals vs Fitted Values",
       x = "Fitted Values", y = "Deviance Residuals") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed")

plot(model, which = 4)

library(pROC)
roc_curve <- roc(behavior_seeg$correct, fitted(model))
plot(roc_curve, main = "ROC Curve")
auc(roc_curve)

min(fitted(model))
```

### Comparison of surprise windows
```{r}
# Initialize vectors to store coefficients for the linear and squared terms
linear_coeffs <- numeric(8)
squared_coeffs <- numeric(8)
model_perf <- numeric(8)

# Loop through each surprise variable
for (i in 0:7) {
  # Create the name of the surprise variable for this iteration
  surprise_var <- paste0("surprise_", i, "_", i+1, "s")
  
  # Construct the formula dynamically, inserting the actual variable name
  formula <- as.formula(paste("correct ~ note_rate + rep +", surprise_var, "+ I(", surprise_var, "^2) + (1|subject)"))
  
  # Run the GLMM for this surprise window
  model <- glmer(formula, data = behavior_seeg, family = binomial(link = 'logit'))
  print(summary(model))
  
  # Extract the coefficients
  coeffs <- summary(model)$coefficients
  
  # Use grep to find the correct row for the surprise variable and its square
  linear_index <- grep(surprise_var, rownames(coeffs))
  squared_index <- grep(paste0("I\\(", surprise_var, "\\^2\\)"), rownames(coeffs))
  model_perf_index <- logLik(model)
  
  # Store the coefficients if found
  if (length(linear_index) > 0) {
    linear_coeffs[i+1] <- coeffs[linear_index, "Estimate"]
  } else {
    warning(paste("Linear coefficient not found for", surprise_var))
  }
  
  if (length(squared_index) > 0) {
    squared_coeffs[i+1] <- coeffs[squared_index, "Estimate"]
  } else {
    warning(paste("Squared coefficient not found for", surprise_var))
  }

  model_perf[i+1] <- model_perf_index
}

# Barplot for linear term coefficients
barplot(linear_coeffs, names.arg = paste0("Window_", 0:7),
        xlab = "Surprise Window", ylab = "Coefficient",
        main = "Coefficients of Surprise Variable (Linear Term)")

# Barplot for squared term coefficients
barplot(squared_coeffs, names.arg = paste0("Window_", 0:7),
        xlab = "Surprise Window", ylab = "Coefficient",
        main = "Coefficients of Surprise Variable (Squared Term)")

plot(model_perf, type = "o", pch = 16, col = "blue",
     xaxt = "n", xlab = "Surprise Window", ylab = "Log Likelihood",
     main = "Model performance")
axis(1, at = 0:7, labels = paste0("Window_", 0:7))
```

### Surprise encoding
# We build an encoding model using surprise to predict RMS in the left hipocampus

## Loading
```{r}
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_left_hippocampus.csv")
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_left_stg.csv")
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_left_prefrontal.csv")
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_heschl.csv")
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_right_hippocampus.csv")
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_hippocampus.csv")
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_left_hippocampus_no_baseline.csv")
# encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_left_hippocampus_diff_baseline.csv")
encoding_data = read.csv("~/These/data/meg_maestro/pac_analysis/seeg/epochs_rms_all_channels/encoding/encoding_data_left_hippocampus_80_150.csv")
encoding_data = encoding_data[!(is.na(encoding_data$correct) | encoding_data$correct==""), ]  # remove empty response, due to multiple button presses with different values
encoding_data = encoding_data[!(is.na(encoding_data$correct2) | encoding_data$correct2==""), ]

encoding_data$subject = as.factor(encoding_data$subject)
encoding_data$electrode = as.factor(encoding_data$electrode)
encoding_data$stim_name = as.factor(encoding_data$stim_name)
encoding_data$note_rate = as.factor(encoding_data$note_rate)
encoding_data$rep = as.factor(encoding_data$rep)
encoding_data$onset = as.factor(encoding_data$onset)

encoding_data$precision_weighted_pe = encoding_data$positive_surprise / encoding_data$uncertainty

for (i in 0:7) {
  # Construct the column name dynamically
  col_name <- paste0("precision_weighted_pe_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  surprise_col_name <- paste0("surprise_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  uncertainty_col_name <- paste0("uncertainty_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[surprise_col_name]] / encoding_data[[uncertainty_col_name]]
}

scale_columns = function(data, columns) {

  for (col in columns) {
    if (col %in% names(data)) {
      scaled_col <- as.vector(scale(data[[col]], scale=TRUE))
      data[[col]] <- scaled_col
    } else {
      warning(paste("Column", col, "not found in the dataframe. Skipping..."))
    }
  }

  return(data)
}
columns_to_scale = names(encoding_data)[sapply(encoding_data, is.numeric)]  # keep numeric columns
columns_to_scale = columns_to_scale[!columns_to_scale %in% c("correct", "correct2")]
encoding_data = scale_columns(encoding_data, columns_to_scale)
encoding_data$rms = encoding_data$rms - min(encoding_data$rms) + 0.01
encoding_data$theta = encoding_data$theta - min(encoding_data$theta) + 0.01
encoding_data$power_stim_freq = encoding_data$power_stim_freq - min(encoding_data$power_stim_freq) + 0.01
encoding_data$high_gamma = encoding_data$high_gamma - min(encoding_data$high_gamma) + 0.01
encoding_data$pac = encoding_data$pac - min(encoding_data$pac) + 0.01
# encoding_data$pac_stim_freq = encoding_data$pac_stim_freq - min(encoding_data$pac_stim_freq) + 0.01
encoding_data$pac4 = encoding_data$pac4 - min(encoding_data$pac4) + 0.01
encoding_data$pac5 = encoding_data$pac5 - min(encoding_data$pac5) + 0.01
encoding_data$pac6 = encoding_data$pac6 - min(encoding_data$pac6) + 0.01
encoding_data$pac7 = encoding_data$pac7 - min(encoding_data$pac7) + 0.01
encoding_data$pac8 = encoding_data$pac8 - min(encoding_data$pac8) + 0.01

for (i in 0:7) {
  # Construct the column name dynamically
  col_name <- paste0("pac_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[col_name]] - min(encoding_data[[col_name]]) + 0.01
  col_name <- paste0("pac_stim_freq_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[col_name]] - min(encoding_data[[col_name]]) + 0.01
  col_name <- paste0("pac4_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[col_name]] - min(encoding_data[[col_name]]) + 0.01
  col_name <- paste0("pac5_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[col_name]] - min(encoding_data[[col_name]]) + 0.01
  col_name <- paste0("pac6_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[col_name]] - min(encoding_data[[col_name]]) + 0.01
  col_name <- paste0("pac7_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[col_name]] - min(encoding_data[[col_name]]) + 0.01
  col_name <- paste0("pac8_", i, "_", i + 1, "s")
  encoding_data[[col_name]] <- encoding_data[[col_name]] - min(encoding_data[[col_name]]) + 0.01
}
```

### GLMM
```{r}
library(lmerTest)  # for significance testing
library(influence.ME)  # for influence diagnostics
library(MuMIn)  # for pseudo-R²

model = glmer(rms ~ note_rate + surprise + I(surprise^2) + (1 | subject) + (1 | subject:electrode), data = encoding_data, family = Gamma(link='log'))
summary(model)

# Deviance residuals
residuals_deviance <- residuals(model, type = "deviance")
fitted_values <- fitted(model)
# Plot deviance residuals vs. fitted values
ggplot(data.frame(fitted_values, residuals_deviance), aes(x = fitted_values, y = residuals_deviance)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "blue", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Deviance Residuals vs Fitted Values",
       x = "Fitted Values",
       y = "Deviance Residuals")
# Histogram of residuals to check their distribution
hist(residuals_deviance, main = "Histogram of Deviance Residuals", xlab = "Deviance Residuals")

# Extract random effects (BLUPs)
ranef_values <- ranef(model, condVar = TRUE)
# QQ plot for the random intercepts for `subject`
qqnorm(ranef_values$subject[[1]], main = "QQ Plot of Random Effects for Subject")
qqline(ranef_values$subject[[1]], col = "blue")
# QQ plot for the random intercepts for `subject:electrode` (nested effects)
qqnorm(ranef_values$`subject:electrode`[[1]], main = "QQ Plot of Random Effects for Electrode within Subject")
qqline(ranef_values$`subject:electrode`[[1]], col = "blue")

# Pearson residuals
residuals_pearson <- residuals(model, type = "pearson")
# Dispersion ratio
dispersion_ratio <- sum(residuals_pearson^2) / df.residual(model)
cat("Dispersion Ratio:", dispersion_ratio)

# Pseudo-R² for model fit
pseudo_r2 <- r.squaredGLMM(model)
cat("Marginal R²:", pseudo_r2[1], "\nConditional R²:", pseudo_r2[2])




# visualize
library(ggeffects)

# Create a data frame of predicted values for surprise
predicted_effects <- ggpredict(model, terms = c("surprise", "note_rate"))

# Plot the predicted effects
ggplot(predicted_effects, aes(x = x, y = predicted, color = group)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) +  # Confidence intervals
  labs(title = "Predicted RMS vs. Surprise (Controlling for Note Rate)",
       x = "Surprise",
       y = "Predicted RMS") +
  theme_minimal()

# Create a new data frame for predictions
surprise_values <- seq(min(encoding_data$surprise), max(encoding_data$surprise), length.out = 100)
note_rates <- levels(encoding_data$note_rate)

# Create a data frame for all combinations of surprise and note_rate
pred_data <- expand.grid(surprise = surprise_values, note_rate = note_rates)

# Calculate the squared surprise term
pred_data$surprise_squared <- pred_data$surprise^2

# Get model coefficients
model_coefs <- fixef(model)

# Calculate predicted RMS based on the model
pred_data$rms_predicted <- exp(
  model_coefs['(Intercept)'] + 
  model_coefs['surprise'] * pred_data$surprise +
  model_coefs['I(surprise^2)'] * pred_data$surprise_squared +
  model_coefs[paste0("note_rate", pred_data$note_rate)]  # Fixed note_rate term
)

# Plot the predicted values with raw data
ggplot(encoding_data, aes(x = surprise, y = rms, color = note_rate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +  # Raw data points
  geom_line(data = pred_data, aes(y = rms_predicted, color = note_rate), size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Predicted RMS vs. Surprise by Note Rate",
       x = "Surprise",
       y = "Predicted RMS") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### mediation analysis
```{r}
library(mediation)

# Mediator model
mediator_model <- glm(rms ~ surprise + I(surprise^2) + note_rate, 
                         data = encoding_data, 
                         family = Gamma(link='log'))
summary(mediator_model)

# Fit the outcome model
outcome_model <- glm(correct ~ rms + I(rms^2) + surprise + I(surprise^2) + note_rate, 
                        data = encoding_data, 
                        family = binomial(link='logit'))
summary(outcome_model)

# Conduct mediation analysis
mediation_result <- mediate(mediator_model, outcome_model, 
                             treat = "surprise", 
                             mediator = "rms", 
                             sims = 1000)

# Summarize and visualize results
summary(mediation_result)
plot(mediation_result)
```

# PAC and encoding
Phase amplitude coupling at the frequency of stimulus (2.5Hz-7.5Hz) and high-gamma (120Hz-140Hz) is associated to correct encoding (PAC at rep1 predicts correct on rep2). 
Theta and high gamma power do not explain this effect.
Theta - high gamma PAC does not explain this effect, neither does power at stim freq, neither do PAC at fixed frequency (4Hz to 8Hz), suggesting an effect locked on the stimulus frequency rather than an intrinsic theta oscillation. 
PAC does not impact correct in the current trial, confirming that it is associated to correct encoding rather than novelty detection or retrieval.
A U-shape relationship between surprise and PAC is close to significant.

### PAC and novelty/retrieval
Theta (broad, 4 to 8Hz) is associated with correct novelty detection (better model than power at stim freq). High gamma may have a slighty negative effect in retrieval. RMS better explains this effect.
Only PAC 7 (and slightly 6) seems to have an effect on correct (instead of correct2), both with a positive effect in novelty and retrieval. Are the maintained encoded sequences played at a fixed rate?

# Phase coherence and encoding
There is no relationship between phase coherence and behavior (novelty, retrieval, encoding), BUT the U-shape with surprise is highly significant (bigger relationship than PAC and surprise), suggesting that low and high surprise increases neural entrainment to the stimulus.

### windows analysis
```{r}
scatterplot(encoding_data_rep1$pac_stim_freq ~ encoding_data_rep1$surprise)
for (i in 0:7) {
  # Dynamically construct the formula as a string and parse it into an expression
  formula_str <- paste0("encoding_data_rep1$pac_stim_freq_", i, "_", i+1, "s ~ encoding_data_rep1$surprise_", i, "_", i+1, "s")
  scatterplot(eval(parse(text = formula_str)))
}

X1_cols <- paste0("surprise_", 0:7, "_", 1:8, "s")
X2_cols <- paste0("rms_", 0:7, "_", 1:8, "s")

# Extract the columns for X1 and X2
X1_data <- encoding_data_rep1[, X1_cols, drop = FALSE]
X2_data <- encoding_data_rep1[, X2_cols, drop = FALSE]

# Initialize a vector to store the coefficients of the second-order term
first_order_coefficients <- numeric(nrow(encoding_data_rep1))
second_order_coefficients <- numeric(nrow(encoding_data_rep1))

# Loop through each row and fit a quadratic polynomial
for (i in 1:nrow(encoding_data_rep1)) {
  # Create a data frame for the X and Y values
  df <- data.frame(
    X = as.numeric(X1_data[i, ]),    # X values for the current row
    Y = as.numeric(X2_data[i, ])     # Y values for the current row
  )
  
  # Fit a quadratic model: Y ~ X + I(X^2)
  fit <- lm(Y ~ X + I(X^2), data = df)
  
  # Extract the coefficient for the X^2 term and store it
  first_order_coefficients[i] <- coef(fit)["X"]
  second_order_coefficients[i] <- coef(fit)["I(X^2)"]
}

# Add the second-order coefficients as a new column to the dataset
encoding_data_rep1$first_order_coefficients <- first_order_coefficients
encoding_data_rep1$second_order_coefficients <- second_order_coefficients
```
